stem: Best guess: prices have risen steadily all year. Which cost flow method reports the **highest** net income?

choices.explanation: Correct. The oldest, cheapest costs go to COGS.
LIFO puts the newest, most expensive costs in COGS — the lowest income.
Average falls between FIFO and LIFO.

choices.text: All methods report the same income
choices.explanation: They report the same only when prices are stable.

explanation: With rising prices, FIFO charges older, lower costs to COGS, producing the highest gross profit and net income (and the highest ending inventory).

stem: A company's year-end physical count is $500,000. Not included: $30,000 of goods purchased FOB shipping point, in transit; $20,000 of goods sold FOB destination, in transit to a customer; $15,000 of goods held on consignment **from** a supplier (included in the count). What is correct inventory?

choices.explanation: This fails to remove the consigned goods, which belong to the supplier.
This omits the goods sold FOB destination, still owned until delivered.
This excludes the purchased goods in transit FOB shipping point, which the buyer owns.

explanation: Add goods the company owns but didn't count (30,000 purchased FOB shipping point; 20,000 sold FOB destination, still in transit) and remove goods it counted but doesn't own (15,000 consigned in): 500,000 + 30,000 + 20,000 − 15,000 = **535,000**.

stem: A company's FIFO inventory is $840,000 and its LIFO inventory is $710,000. What is the LIFO reserve?

choices.explanation: The reserve is a difference, not a sum.
By convention the reserve is FIFO minus LIFO — positive when prices have risen.
That is the LIFO inventory itself.

explanation: LIFO reserve = FIFO − LIFO = **130,000**. Adding the reserve to LIFO inventory approximates FIFO for comparisons.

stem: Beginning inventory 200 units at $20; purchases of 300 units at $22 and then 250 units at $25. At year-end 350 units remain (periodic system). What is ending inventory under FIFO?

choices.explanation: This is LIFO ending inventory (200 × 20 + 150 × 22 = 7,300).
This is weighted average (16,850 ÷ 750 = 22.4667 × 350).
This values all 350 units at the latest $25 cost, but only 250 units were bought at $25.

explanation: Goods available = 16,850 for 750 units. FIFO leaves the newest costs: 250 × $25 + 100 × $22 = **8,450**.

stem: Beginning inventory 200 units at $20; purchases of 300 units at $22 and then 250 units at $25. At year-end 350 units remain (periodic system). What is cost of goods sold under LIFO?

choices.explanation: This is FIFO COGS (16,850 − 8,450).
That is LIFO ending inventory, not COGS.
This is weighted-average COGS.

stem: Beginning inventory 200 units at $20; purchases of 300 units at $22 and then 250 units at $25. At year-end 350 units remain (periodic system). What is ending inventory under the weighted-average method (rounded to the nearest dollar)?

choices.explanation: This uses a simple average of the three unit costs ($22.33) instead of weighting by units.
This is FIFO ending inventory, not weighted average.
This is LIFO ending inventory, not weighted average.

explanation: Weighted-average cost = 16,850 ÷ 750 units = $22.4667. Ending inventory = 350 × 22.4667 = **7,863**.

stem: Beginning inventory: 100 units at $8. Jan 10: bought 100 units at $9. Jan 15: sold 150 units. Jan 20: bought 100 units at $10. What is ending inventory under **perpetual** LIFO?

choices.explanation: This is periodic LIFO (100 × 8 + 50 × 9), which ignores when the sale occurred.
Correct. The Jan 15 sale used 100 @ 9 and 50 @ 8; remaining 50 @ 8 plus 100 @ 10.
This values all ending units at the latest cost.
This is FIFO: the sale uses 100 @ 8 and 50 @ 9, leaving 50 @ 9 + 100 @ 10.

explanation: Perpetual LIFO applies LIFO at each sale. Jan 15 sale of 150: 100 @ $9 + 50 @ $8. Left: 50 @ $8. Add Jan 20: 100 @ $10. Ending = 400 + 1,000 = **1,400**. (Periodic LIFO would give 1,250.)

stem: Which cost is **excluded** from the cost of inventory purchased by a retailer?

choices.explanation: Freight-in is a cost of getting goods to their saleable location.
Duties are part of acquisition cost.

choices.text: Freight-out to deliver goods to customers
choices.explanation: Correct. Delivery to customers is a selling expense.

choices.text: Purchase price net of cash discounts taken
choices.explanation: The net purchase price is the core inventory cost.

explanation: Inventory includes costs to bring goods to their existing condition and location (price, freight-in, duties, handling). Freight-out is a selling expense.

stem: On December 28, Seller shipped goods costing $40,000 to Buyer, FOB destination; they arrived January 3. On December 30, Buyer also received goods it holds on consignment from Seller worth $25,000. Which amounts should Seller include in its December 31 inventory?

choices.explanation: Seller still owns both shipments.
The consigned goods also still belong to Seller.
FOB destination goods in transit also still belong to Seller.
Correct. Title hadn't passed on the FOB destination shipment, and consignors own consigned goods.

explanation: FOB destination: title passes on arrival (January 3) — Seller's inventory at year-end. Consigned goods remain the consignor's inventory. Total **65,000**.

stem: A company adopted dollar-value LIFO at the start of Year 1, when inventory was $80,000 (index 1.00). At the end of Year 1, inventory at year-end prices was $99,000 and the price index was 1.10. What is ending inventory under dollar-value LIFO?

choices.explanation: That is inventory at current prices, not LIFO.
That is inventory at base-year prices, before pricing the new layer.
This applies the index to the base layer (80,000 × 1.10).

stem: During a year of rising prices, a LIFO company sold more units than it purchased, dipping into layers acquired years ago. What is the effect?

choices.text: COGS is lower and gross profit higher than otherwise
choices.explanation: Correct. Old, low costs flow into COGS — a LIFO liquidation.

choices.text: Cost of goods sold is higher than normal
choices.explanation: Old layers carry lower costs, reducing COGS.

choices.text: There is no effect because LIFO always matches current costs
choices.explanation: A liquidation breaks that matching.

choices.text: The company must switch to FIFO
choices.explanation: No such requirement exists.

explanation: A LIFO liquidation releases old, low-cost layers into COGS, inflating gross profit (and taxes). Material effects are disclosed.

stem: Which statement about LIFO is correct?

choices.text: IFRS permits LIFO for companies in inflationary economies
choices.explanation: IFRS prohibits LIFO entirely.

choices.text: A company using LIFO for federal income taxes must also use LIFO for financial reporting
choices.explanation: Correct. The LIFO conformity rule.

choices.text: LIFO periodic and LIFO perpetual always produce the same ending inventory
choices.explanation: They can differ because perpetual applies LIFO at each sale.

choices.text: LIFO reports the most current costs on the balance sheet
choices.explanation: LIFO leaves the oldest costs on the balance sheet.

explanation: The LIFO conformity rule (IRC §472) requires book use of LIFO when it is used for tax. IFRS prohibits LIFO.

stem: Goods available for sale were $600,000. Ending inventory was understated by $15,000 because goods in a remote warehouse were not counted. What is the effect on current-year cost of goods sold and net income (ignore taxes)?

choices.explanation: Reversed — understating ending inventory overstates COGS.
Ending inventory directly determines COGS.

choices.text: COGS overstated by $15,000; net income understated by $15,000
choices.explanation: Correct. COGS = goods available − ending inventory.

choices.text: COGS overstated by $30,000; net income understated by $30,000
choices.explanation: The error doubles only across two years' cumulative misstatement if uncorrected — not in one year.

explanation: COGS = 600,000 − ending inventory. Understating ending inventory by 15,000 overstates COGS by 15,000 and understates net income by 15,000.

stem: On December 30 a seller ships goods FOB destination; they arrive January 3. Whose December 31 inventory includes them?

choices.explanation: Correct. Under FOB destination, title passes when the goods arrive.
The buyer gets title on arrival.
Carriers don't own goods they transport.
Someone always owns the goods.

explanation: FOB shipping point: title passes at shipment. FOB destination: title passes on delivery.

stem: A manufacturer ships goods on consignment to a retailer, which has sold none of them at year-end. The goods are included in:

choices.explanation: The consignee holds but doesn't own the goods.
Correct. The consignor keeps title until the goods are sold.
Only the owner reports them.
The consignor still owns them.

explanation: Consigned goods remain in the consignor's inventory until sold to an end customer.

stem: A company uses a perpetual moving-average system. It had 100 units at $10, bought 100 at $12, sold 150, then bought 50 at $14. What is ending inventory?

choices.explanation: That uses FIFO for the remaining units.
That uses the periodic average of all purchases.
Correct. Average 11 after the purchase; 50 left × 11 = 550, plus 700 = 1,250.
That values all 100 units at the last cost.

explanation: Moving average recomputes the unit cost after each purchase: (1,000 + 1,200) ÷ 200 = 11.

stem: Under dollar-value LIFO, base-year inventory is $100,000 (index 1.00). Year 1 ending inventory at current cost is $132,000, and the year-end index is 1.10. What is Year 1 ending inventory?

choices.explanation: That is current cost, not LIFO.
The new layer is priced at the current index.
Only the increment over the base is indexed.

explanation: Deflate ending inventory to base-year cost, find the layer, and reprice each layer at its own index.

stem: Which cost is included in the cost of inventory purchased for resale?

choices.explanation: Correct. Costs to bring goods to their location and condition are inventory costs.
Shipping to customers is a selling expense.
Commissions are selling expenses.
Interest on routine inventory isn't capitalized.

explanation: Inventory cost includes purchase price, freight-in and other costs to get goods ready for sale.

stem: Beginning inventory is 100 units at $10. Purchases: 200 at $13 and 100 at $16. Ending inventory is 150 units. What is ending inventory under periodic weighted average?

choices.explanation: That's the FIFO result.
That's the LIFO result.
Use the weighted average.
Correct. $13 average × 150.

explanation: Weighted average cost = $5,200 ÷ 400 = $13 per unit.

stem: A company buys goods FOB shipping point. They ship December 29 and arrive January 4. Whose year-end inventory includes them?

choices.explanation: Correct. Title passed at shipment.
Title passed at shipment.
They're owned by the buyer.
Title passes in full.

explanation: Under FOB shipping point, title passes to the buyer when goods are shipped.

stem: A factory runs at 60% of normal capacity. How is fixed overhead allocated to inventory?

choices.text: All of it, over actual output
choices.explanation: That inflates unit cost.
Correct. Unallocated overhead is a period cost.

choices.text: None of it; it's all expensed
choices.explanation: Fixed overhead is a product cost.
It's expensed, not deferred.

explanation: Fixed overhead is allocated based on normal capacity; unallocated overhead from low production is expensed.

stem: A jeweler sells unique, high-value pieces. Which cost flow method fits best?

choices.explanation: Units aren't interchangeable.
Units aren't interchangeable.
Correct. Each item's cost is tracked.
Units aren't interchangeable.

explanation: Specific identification suits distinguishable, high-value items.

stem: A company uses LIFO for its tax return. What does the LIFO conformity rule require?

choices.explanation: The rule is the reverse.
The rule binds the books.

choices.text: Disclosure of the LIFO reserve only
choices.explanation: LIFO must be used.
Correct. Book and tax must both use LIFO.

explanation: The LIFO conformity rule requires a taxpayer using LIFO for tax to use LIFO for financial reporting.
